mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about the octet rule is **incorrect**?

options.A: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons so that they have eight electrons in their valence shell.
options.B: Hydrogen can achieve an octet by sharing two electrons with another atom.
options.C: The octet rule is applicable to most main‑group elements in the second period of the periodic table.
options.D: Ions formed by metals usually lose electrons to attain a noble‑gas configuration.

mcqs.answer: Hydrogen can achieve an octet by sharing two electrons with another atom.
mcqs.explanation: Hydrogen follows the duet rule, not the octet rule, because its 1s orbital can hold only two electrons. Therefore statement B is false, while the other statements correctly describe the octet rule or its typical applicability. Recognising this common misconception helps avoid applying the octet rule to hydrogen and helium.

mcqs.question: Which of the following correctly represents the Lewis symbol for a chlorine (Cl) atom?

options.A: Cl with a single dot above the symbol
options.B: Cl with a pair of dots on the left side
options.C: Cl surrounded by seven single dots
options.D: Cl with three pairs of dots and one single dot

mcqs.answer: Cl surrounded by seven single dots
mcqs.explanation: Chlorine belongs to group 17 and has seven valence electrons. In a Lewis symbol these are shown as seven single dots placed around the element symbol. Option C displays exactly seven dots, whereas the other options show an incorrect number or arrangement of electrons.

mcqs.question: Two Lewis structures are drawn for the molecule CO₂. Which one correctly represents the molecule according to the octet rule?

options.A: C double‑bonded to each O, with each O bearing two lone pairs and carbon having no lone pairs.
options.B: C single‑bonded to each O, with each O bearing three lone pairs and carbon bearing one lone pair.
options.C: C triple‑bonded to one O and single‑bonded to the other O, with appropriate lone pairs on O atoms.
options.D: C double‑bonded to one O and single‑bonded to the other O, with carbon bearing a positive charge.

mcqs.answer: C double‑bonded to each O, with each O bearing two lone pairs and carbon having no lone pairs.
mcqs.explanation: In CO₂ each oxygen needs eight electrons and carbon also needs eight. The structure with double bonds (option A) gives carbon six valence electrons from the two bonds, plus two more from the shared pairs, completing its octet. Each oxygen receives two electrons from the double bond and has two lone pairs, also satisfying the octet rule. Options B, C, and D either give atoms an incomplete octet or introduce unnecessary charges.

mcqs.question: Which of the following molecules **does not** obey the octet rule?
mcqs.explanation: Boron in BF₃ has only six valence electrons after forming three covalent bonds with fluorine; it does not achieve an octet, illustrating a well‑known limitation of the octet rule for elements in period 2 with less than eight electrons. CO₂, NH₃, and CH₄ all have complete octets for the central atom, so they obey the rule.
